lessons.title: The room becomes a band
lessons.intention: We are learning what each player is responsible for in a band.
criteria: I can name my role in the ensemble and say who I have to listen to.
steps: Instrument allocation. Every student is placed on a part and the four ensemble roles are named in the room: melody, harmony, bass, groove.
The class plays a single four-chord loop together, badly, then fixes it one role at a time.
Students record in their books which role they are carrying and who else is carrying it.
resources: Room kit: guitars, bass, keys, drums, vocal PA.
lessons.enduring: A band works because each player knows their role, their function and their balance.

body.lead: We are learning what each player is responsible for in a band.

The whole room plays one four-chord loop together. It will not sound good the first time. It is then fixed one role at a time, so you hear what each role was doing wrong.
Write down which role you are carrying and who else in the room is carrying it. Those are the people you listen to first.

criteria: I can name my role in the ensemble.
I can say who I have to listen to.

lessons.title: Safe practice, set-up and pack-down
lessons.intention: We are learning to work safely and respectfully in a music room.
criteria: I can warm up, set up and pack down without being told each step.
steps: Warm-up routine for voice and for hands, taught as a routine to be repeated every lesson from now on.
Posture, volume and hearing. Cable, amp and stand handling, and the pack-down order for the room.
The protocols of working with other people's instruments: hygiene, asking, and reporting damage.

I can set up and pack down the room in the right order.

lessons.title: flat.io opens, and the weekly aural routine begins
lessons.intention: We are learning to identify the elements of music by ear and write what we hear.
criteria: I can hear the metre of an excerpt and write it down correctly.
steps: Students log in to flat.io and set up the class notebook. Nothing is composed: this is where bookwork lives.
The weekly aural routine starts and does not stop for the rest of the year. Ten minutes: metre, beat and pulse, identified by ear and written up.
Note entry drill: pitches placed on the stave from dictation, checked against the answer.
lessons.enduring: Aural skill improves through short, regular, structured practice.

body.lead: We are learning to identify the elements of music by ear and write down what we hear.

clauses.text: flat.io opens today and the class notebook is set up. Nothing is composed in it yet: this is where your bookwork lives for the rest of the year.
The weekly aural routine starts now and does not stop. Ten minutes on metre, beat and pulse, heard first and named second.
Take the note entry drill: pitches placed on the stave from dictation, then checked against the answer.

criteria: I can hear the metre of an excerpt.
I can write down what I heard correctly.

lessons.title: The four-chord loop, heard then played
lessons.intention: We are learning to hear a chord progression and play it back.
criteria: I can hear the four-chord loop, play it, and say where it repeats.
steps: The four-chord loop (I, V, vi, IV) heard across a set of songs chosen from the register, and identified by ear before it is named.
The loop sung, then played, in two keys.
Students identify by ear where the loop starts again, and mark the change points on the chart.
resources: Listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: The same small pattern sits underneath a great many songs.

body.lead: We are learning to hear a chord progression and play it back.

clauses.text: The four-chord loop is heard across a set of songs before it is named. You work out that they share something, then you are told what it is: I, V, vi, IV.
The loop is sung first and then played, in two keys, so that it stays a shape in your hands rather than a set of letters on a page.
Find by ear where the loop starts again, and mark the change points on your chart.

criteria: I can hear the four-chord loop and play it.
I can say where it starts again.

guide.brief: Two of the three songs, walked through. Press a name to play it from the top, or press a time to drop straight into that moment.

cues.text: The bass arrives playing the whole loop on its own: **D, A, Bm, G**, one bar each. This is the clearest the four chords ever get, so start your counting here.
Bar one again. The loop comes round every eight and a half seconds, so it restarts again at 0:35, at 0:44 and at 0:52.
Well into the song now, and the chords have not moved once. Everything that has changed has been layered over the top of them.
The biggest the arrangement gets. Same four chords, same eight and a half seconds. Nothing underneath has changed at all.
The piano has the loop before anything else happens: **A, E, F#m, D**. Faster than the U2, so the loop comes round every seven seconds.
Bar one, and the singing starts on the same beat. This is the only time in the song they line up, which is exactly why you cannot use the voice to find the loop.
Bar one. Listen for the second chord: the bass note walks down instead of jumping, and the chord is still V.
Still the same four chords. This song gets bigger by adding to the loop, never by changing it.

explain.title: I, V, vi and IV: what the numbers are doing

body.p: Every major key has seven chords built on its seven notes, and they are numbered from the bottom up in roman numerals. In C major, chord I is C, chord V is G, chord vi is A minor and chord IV is F. Change key and every letter changes, but the numbers do not: in G major those same four chords are G, D, E minor and C. That is the whole reason for numbering them. **A letter tells you what a chord is called. A number tells you what it is doing in the key.**
Each of the four has a job you can hear.

ul: **I is home.** It is where the loop feels settled, and where a song most often stops.
**V pulls.** It is the most restless of the four, and it wants to fall back to I.
**IV moves away**, but without much tension, which is why it can sit under a chorus for a long time without becoming uncomfortable.
**vi is the minor one.** It is I with the light off: it shares two of its three notes, so it sounds like home and feels nothing like it.

body.p: Put them in that order, I, V, vi, IV, and the loop leaves home, pulls, darkens and drifts, then starts again. It never quite closes. That is why it can run under a whole song without wearing out, and it is why you have heard it under so many songs already without noticing that it was the same four chords.

Do not try to count the chords. Count four, steadily, and listen for the moment the harmony brightens and settles. That is I, and that is bar one of the loop. The hard part is that a singer will often come in partway through, so the start of the singing and the start of the loop are rarely the same moment. Follow the chords, not the voice.

lessons.title: Reading a chart, reading a lead sheet
lessons.contentPoint: Performing from a range of scores
lessons.intention: We are learning to read the scores a band actually uses.
criteria: I can follow a lead sheet through a whole song without losing my place.
steps: The difference between a chord chart and a lead sheet, taught by playing from both.
Repeat signs, first and second time bars, and the road map of a song.
Students follow a full lead sheet while the recording plays and mark where they lost their place.
resources: Printed lead sheets for the class repertoire.
lessons.enduring: Reading a chart is a skill in its own right, and it comes before writing one.

body.lead: We are learning to read the scores a band actually uses.

clauses.text: The difference between a chord chart and a lead sheet is taught by playing from both of them, not by looking at them side by side.
Repeat signs, first and second time bars, and the road map of a song. This is how you know where to go next without anyone calling it out.
Follow a full lead sheet while the recording plays, and mark the bar where you lost your place. That bar is the one to practise.

criteria: I can follow a lead sheet through a whole song.
I can find my place again when I lose it.

patched.text: Printed lead sheets for the class repertoire

lessons.title: AT1 issued, and the first performance to the room
lessons.contentPoint: Singing with melodic and harmonic awareness
lessons.intention: We are learning what AT1 asks for and starting to perform to the room.
criteria: I can perform a short piece to the class and say what I would fix next time.
steps: Assessment Task 1 issued: a performance of a chosen cover, solo or ensemble, due Week 8. The notification and criteria are read together and the criteria language is used from here on.
The performance cycle opens. Every student plays or sings something short to the room this lesson, unmarked.
Whole-class singing with the band, attending to tuning against the harmony.
lessons.enduring: Performing to the room is a routine, so that the assessment is not the first time.

body.lead: We are learning what AT1 asks for and starting to perform to the room.

clauses.text: AT1 is issued today: a cover, solo or in a group, performed in Week 8. The notification and the criteria are read together, and their words are the words we use from here on.
The performance cycle opens. Everybody plays or sings something short to the room today. It is not marked, and it is not optional.
Whole-class singing with the band behind it, listening for whether you are in tune with the harmony rather than only with yourself.

criteria: I can perform something short to the class.
I can say one thing I would fix next time.

lessons.title: Balance in the room
lessons.intention: We are learning to balance an ensemble so the important part is heard.
criteria: I can adjust my volume so that the part that matters can be heard.
steps: The band plays the class piece three times: once too loud, once with the melody buried, once balanced. Students name the difference.
Amp and PA levels set as a decision rather than by habit.
Each section rehearses alone, then against one other section.
lessons.enduring: Balance is a musical decision made by the players, not by the desk.

body.lead: We are learning to balance an ensemble so the part that matters can be heard.

clauses.text: The class piece is played three times: once too loud, once with the melody buried, once balanced. You name the difference rather than being told it.
Amp and PA levels are then set as a decision. Where the knob was left last time is not a reason.
Rehearse with your section alone, then against one other section, and fix the balance by changing your own volume first.

criteria: I can hear when the important part is buried.
I can adjust my own volume to fix it.

lessons.title: Singing the top line, playing the parts
lessons.contentPoint: Singing with melodic and harmonic awareness
lessons.intention: We are learning to sing and play with melodic and harmonic awareness.
criteria: I can hold my line while another part sounds against it.
steps: Whole-class singing of the melody with harmonic accompaniment, attending to tuning and to where the harmony pulls the melody.
Two-part singing on a short section, so that harmonic awareness is experienced rather than described.
Each student then plays the melody on their instrument.
lessons.enduring: Hearing your own part inside the harmony is what makes an ensemble work.

body.lead: We are learning to sing and play with melodic and harmonic awareness.

clauses.text: The whole class sings the melody with the harmony underneath it, listening for the places where the harmony pulls the tune somewhere you did not expect.
Take a short section in two parts. Harmonic awareness is not something you can be told about; it is what happens when the other line is in your ear.
Then play the melody on your own instrument, and keep it in tune with the part sounding against it.

criteria: I can hold my line while another part sounds against it.
I can hear where the harmony changes what the melody does.

lessons.title: Aural routine: metre, beat and the chord change
lessons.intention: We are learning to hear where harmony changes and to write down what we hear.
criteria: I can mark the beat a chord changes on and notate a two-bar rhythm.
steps: Aural routine, week 3: identifying where the chord changes fall against the beat.
Rhythmic dictation of a two-bar pattern from the class repertoire, written into flat.io.
Students sing back a four-note melodic pattern and then play it.
lessons.enduring: The ear is trained by naming what it already hears.

body.lead: We are learning to hear where the harmony changes and to write down what we hear.

clauses.text: Week 3 of the routine: finding where the chord changes fall against the beat. Not which chord yet, just which beat.
Write a two-bar rhythm from the class repertoire into your aural notebook, from dictation.
Sing back a four-note pattern and then play it. Singing it first is the part that makes the playing work.

criteria: I can mark the beat a chord changes on.
I can notate a two-bar rhythm from dictation.

lessons.title: Cover versus original: the one changed element
lessons.intention: We are learning to compare two interpretations of the same song.
criteria: I can identify the element a cover changed and describe the change accurately.
steps: A cover and its original side by side. Students name every difference, then keep the one that matters most.
Repeated with a pair whose changed element is different, so the method transfers rather than the answer.
Class builds the comparison table that will be used for the rest of the block.
resources: Cover and original pairs from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: A cover changes one thing at a time and leaves the rest alone, which is what makes it analysable.

body.lead: We are learning to compare two interpretations of the same song.

clauses.text: A cover and its original are played side by side. The class names every difference it can hear, then throws out all but the one that matters.
It is done again on a pair whose changed element is a different one, so what you take away is the method and not the answer.
Fill in the class comparison table for both pairs, and write the changed element as a sentence rather than a word.

criteria: I can identify the element a cover changed.
I can describe the change accurately.

lessons.title: ALARM and the well-formed dot point
lessons.intention: We are learning to write an analytical dot point that explains rather than lists.
criteria: I can write a dot point that names a feature, locates it and says why it is there.
steps: ALARM introduced as a visible classroom tool at the describe to explain rung, and it stays on the wall.
The well-formed dot point modelled then built: the feature, what it sounds like and where, and why it is there.
Students write three dot points on one comparison and mark each other's against the model.
resources: Model dot points, strong and weak.
lessons.enduring: Music applies ALARM to build well-formed dot points, not paragraphs.

body.lead: We are learning to write an analytical dot point that explains rather than lists.

clauses.text: ALARM goes on the wall today at the describe to explain rung, and it stays there for the rest of the year.
The well-formed dot point is modelled and then built in three parts: the feature, what it sounds like and where, and why it is there.
Write three dot points on one comparison, swap, and mark each other's against the model rather than against what you thought of the song.

criteria: I can name a feature and locate it.
I can say why it is there.

patched.text: Model dot points, strong and weak

lessons.title: AT1 repertoire locked, and why this song
lessons.contentPoint: Interpreting a range of genres and styles
lessons.intention: We are learning that a performance is an interpretation made for an audience.
criteria: I can explain why I chose this song and what I want the audience to hear.
steps: AT1 repertoire locked. Each student or group states the song, the version and the parts.
The same song discussed from three positions: what the composer wrote, what the performer decided, and what the audience receives.
Interpretation as a decision: two performances of one piece in different genres, and what each is for.
lessons.enduring: Composer, performer and audience are three different positions on the same work.

body.lead: We are learning that a performance is an interpretation made for an audience.

clauses.text: AT1 repertoire is locked today. You state the song, which version of it, and who is playing what. After today it does not change.
One song is discussed from three positions: what the writer put down, what the performer decided, and what the audience actually receives.
Write why you chose this song and what you want the room to hear in it. You will be held to that in Week 8.

criteria: I can explain why I chose this song.
I can say what I want the audience to hear.

lessons.title: What the studio did
lessons.intention: We are learning how recording technology changes what we hear in a song.
criteria: I can identify a production decision and explain its effect on the listener.
steps: Production compared as well as performance: reverb, compression, doubling, tuning and how each changes what the listener believes about the room.
How a song is adapted for a different audience or purpose, and what is lost and gained each time.
Students identify one production decision in their own AT1 recording that they cannot reproduce live, and plan around it.
resources: Studio versus live recordings of one song.
lessons.enduring: Technology is part of the interpretation, not a layer added on top of it.

body.lead: We are learning how recording technology changes what we hear in a song.

clauses.text: Reverb, compression, doubling and tuning, heard one at a time. Each of them changes what you believe about the room the singer was standing in.
The same song adapted for a different audience or purpose, and what is lost and gained each time it moves.
Find one production decision in your own AT1 recording that you cannot reproduce live, and plan what you will do instead.

criteria: I can identify a production decision in a recording.
I can explain what it does to the listener.

patched.text: Studio and live recordings of one song

lessons.title: A cover from outside the anglophone mainstream
lessons.intention: We are learning that different musical cultures value different qualities.
criteria: I can describe what this style values and compare it with what I expected.
steps: One cover studied from outside the anglophone mainstream, chosen from the register. The global music culture area is first met here.
What is aesthetically valued in this style, and how that differs from what the class assumed.
Written comparison of the two aesthetics, one dot point each.
resources: Global music culture listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: Aesthetic judgement is cultural, and naming that is part of listening well.

body.lead: We are learning that different musical cultures value different qualities.

clauses.text: One cover from outside the anglophone mainstream: Angélique Kidjo's reading of Once in a Lifetime, a song the Talking Heads recorded first. This is where the global music culture area starts for the year.
What this style values, and how that differs from what you assumed music of this kind was for. Name the difference rather than ranking the two.
Write one dot point comparing the two aesthetics. Which one you prefer is not the question and is not the answer.

criteria: I can describe what this style values.
I can compare it with what I expected to hear.

lessons.title: Playing the difference
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse the elements of music in the repertoire we perform.
criteria: I can change one element in my performance and describe the effect.
steps: The class plays one section of a song twice, changing a single element each time, and analyses the result as performers rather than listeners.
Discussion: which of these changes would you keep, and what does that tell you about the song?
Students annotate their own AT1 chart with the elements they intend to change.
lessons.enduring: The analysis a performer does is the same analysis a listener does, done with the hands.

body.lead: We are learning to analyse the elements of music in the repertoire we perform.

clauses.text: One section is played twice, changing a single element each time. You are analysing it from the inside, as the player making the change.
Which of those changes would you keep? What you keep says something about the song, and saying it out loud is the analysis.
Annotate your own AT1 chart with the elements you intend to change, and be able to say why for each one.

criteria: I can change one element in my performance.
I can describe the effect of the change.

lessons.title: Rehearsal that fixes rather than describes
lessons.intention: We are learning to rehearse in a way that changes the performance.
criteria: I can name a problem in musical terms and run a rehearsal step that fixes it.
steps: Rehearsal technique taught explicitly: isolate, slow, repeat, restore. Modelled by the teacher on a real problem in the room.
The vocabulary of rehearsal: the terms used to say what to do next, not to describe what went wrong.
Each group runs one rehearsal cycle on their own AT1 piece and logs what they fixed.
resources: Practice rooms and the main room.
lessons.enduring: Rehearsal is a technique with steps, not simply playing the piece again.

body.lead: We are learning to rehearse in a way that changes the performance.

clauses.text: Rehearsal technique is taught out loud: isolate, slow, repeat, restore. It is modelled on a real problem in this room, not on a hypothetical one.
The vocabulary of rehearsal is the vocabulary of what to do next. Saying that it went badly is not a rehearsal step.
Run one full cycle on your own AT1 piece and log what you fixed, in those terms.

criteria: I can name a problem in musical terms.
I can run a rehearsal step that fixes it.

patched.text: Practice rooms and the main room

lessons.title: Recording a rehearsal and listening back
lessons.contentPoint: Technology to record and mix performances
lessons.intention: We are learning to use recording to hear our own playing honestly.
criteria: I can record a rehearsal and identify two specific things to change.
steps: The rehearsal recorded on the room's interface or an iPad, then played back for balance, tuning and timing.
Basic mixing decisions: level, pan, and why the vocal needs space.
Students write two dot points on their own recording.
lessons.enduring: You cannot fix what you have not heard from outside.

body.lead: We are learning to use recording to hear our own playing honestly.

clauses.text: The rehearsal is recorded on the room's interface or an iPad, then played straight back for balance, tuning and timing.
The mixing decisions that matter at this stage: level, pan, and why the vocal has to be given room to sit in.
Write two dot points on your own recording. Not on how it felt to play, on what is actually on the recording.

criteria: I can record a rehearsal and play it back.
I can identify two specific things to change.

lessons.title: Feedback round 1
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate our own performance and set a target from it.
criteria: I can identify one specific technical target from watching myself back.
steps: First recorded feedback round. Each student or group performs to the class and receives structured feedback against the AT1 criteria.
Feedback given in the criteria's own language, one strength and one next step.
Students set a written target for the fortnight.
lessons.enduring: Evaluation is only useful when it produces a next step.

body.lead: We are learning to evaluate our own performance and set a target from it.

clauses.text: The first recorded feedback round. You perform to the class and take feedback against the AT1 criteria, on video, so that you can watch it back.
Feedback is given in the criteria's own words: one strength and one next step. Nothing else gets said.
Watch yourself back and write one technical target for the fortnight. One, and specific enough to check.

criteria: I can watch myself back and judge it against the criteria.
I can set one specific target from what I saw.

lessons.title: Arrangement choices: why this song, played this way
lessons.intention: We are learning to make and defend arrangement decisions.
criteria: I can explain one arrangement decision and what it does for the audience.
steps: The arrangement examined as a set of decisions: key, tempo, instrumentation, what is cut and what is repeated.
Personal style discussed through experimentation: two students play the same phrase and the class names the difference.
Each group states the purpose of their performance and who it is for.
lessons.enduring: Why this song, played this way, for this room, is the question a performer answers.

body.lead: We are learning to make and defend arrangement decisions.

clauses.text: The arrangement broken into the decisions it is made of: key, tempo, instrumentation, what gets cut and what gets repeated.
Two players take the same phrase and the room names the difference between them. That difference is personal style, and it is arrived at by trying things.
State what your performance is for and who it is for, then name one arrangement decision that serves it.

criteria: I can explain one arrangement decision.
I can say what it does for the audience.

lessons.title: Sharing a recording: copyright, permission and identity
lessons.contentPoint: Information, identity and copyright when sharing
lessons.intention: We are learning the protocols that apply when a performance is shared.
criteria: I can say what I must check before a recording of my group is posted.
steps: The moment a student wants to post the rehearsal: copyright, permission, attribution and what a school account may and may not publish.
Identity and information online, including who else is in the recording and whether they agreed.
The school's protocols applied to a real example from this class.
lessons.enduring: Copyright and consent are part of performing, not paperwork bolted on afterwards.

body.lead: We are learning the protocols that apply when a performance is shared.

clauses.text: The moment somebody wants to post the rehearsal video. Copyright, permission, attribution, and what a school account may and may not publish.
Identity and information online, including who else is in the recording and whether they agreed to be in it.
Check your own group's recording against the protocols and write down what would have to happen before it could be posted anywhere.

criteria: I can say what must be checked before a recording of my group is posted.
I can write a correct attribution.

lessons.title: Feedback round 2, and the run-through
lessons.intention: We are learning to show measurable improvement between two feedback rounds.
criteria: I can show what improved since round one and name what I changed to do it.
steps: Second recorded feedback round, against the target set in Week 6.
Full run-through in performance order, with entries, endings and changeovers rehearsed.
Final rehearsal log entry: what changed between round one and round two.
resources: Video from round one for comparison.
lessons.enduring: Improvement that cannot be pointed to has not been evidenced.

body.lead: We are learning to show measurable improvement between two feedback rounds.

clauses.text: The second recorded round, against the target you set in Week 6. The video from round one is played beside it.
A full run-through in performance order, with entries, endings and changeovers rehearsed. Week 8 is not the day to work out who is going first.
Write the last rehearsal log entry: what changed between round one and round two, and what you did to change it.

criteria: I can show what improved since round one.
I can name what I changed to do it.

lessons.title: AT1 performances, day 1
lessons.intention: We are learning to perform with technical and expressive control under assessment conditions.
criteria: I can perform my chosen cover with control of tone, timing and expression.
steps: Assessment Task 1 performances begin. Technical and expressive control assessed against the criteria issued in Week 2.
Audience protocol taught and enforced: how a class listens to a classmate.
Marking notes taken live against the criteria.
lessons.enduring: Control of the instrument is what lets an interpretation be heard.

body.lead: We are learning to perform with technical and expressive control under assessment conditions.

clauses.text: AT1 performances begin. You go on in the running order and play the cover you locked in Week 4.
Audience protocol applies and is enforced: how this class listens while one of its own is playing.
Technical and expressive control, marked against the criteria you were given in Week 2. Nothing in them has changed since.

criteria: I can perform my cover with control of tone and timing.
I can shape it expressively rather than only get through it.

lessons.title: AT1 performances, day 2, and staging
lessons.intention: We are learning how staging and set-up affect what an audience receives.
criteria: I can set up, perform and finish in a way that communicates to the room.
steps: Remaining performances. Each is staged rather than played from a seat: entry, set-up, the piece, the ending, the acknowledgement.
The effect of the set-up on communication discussed after each performance.
Room reconfigured once during the lesson so the class experiences the difference.
lessons.enduring: Where you stand and how you finish are part of the performance.

body.lead: We are learning how staging and set-up affect what an audience receives.

clauses.text: The remaining performances. Each one is staged rather than played from a seat: you walk on, set up, play, finish, and acknowledge the room.
The room is reconfigured once during the lesson, so you hear what the same performance does from a different set-up.
Marked against the same criteria as day one, and marking notes are taken live, while you play.

criteria: I can set up, perform and finish without being prompted.
I can say what the staging did for the audience.

patched.text: PA, staging area and music stands

lessons.title: Reflection against the criteria
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate our own performance against its stated intent.
criteria: I can judge whether my performance communicated what I intended, with evidence.
steps: Written reflection immediately after performing, against the same criteria the task was marked on.
Students state what they set out to communicate and whether it landed.
Reflections filed for the process log, which opens formally next week.
lessons.enduring: Reflection is against intent, not against how the student felt.

body.lead: We are learning to evaluate our own performance against what we set out to do.

clauses.text: The written reflection happens now, while it is still fresh, and against the same criteria the task was marked on.
Watch each other's video once and point to the moment where the intention is audible, or to the place where it stops being audible.
Judge whether your performance communicated what you intended, with evidence from the video. File it: the process log opens next week and this is its first entry.

criteria: I can judge my performance against what I intended.
I can point to evidence for that judgement.

lessons.title: Verse and chorus taken apart
lessons.intention: We are learning how a song is built out of sections.
criteria: I can map a song's structure and say what changes at each section boundary.
steps: Verse and chorus structure taken apart in the term's own repertoire: what changes at the chorus, and how the song signals it.
Macrostructure mapped on the board for three songs, then compared.
Students map the structure of their own AT1 song.
lessons.enduring: A song's shape is a decision, and the listener hears the decision.

body.lead: We are learning how a song is built out of sections.

clauses.text: Verse and chorus pulled apart in this term's own repertoire. What actually changes at the chorus, and how the song tells you it is coming.
Three songs mapped on the board and then compared, so that the shape reads as a decision somebody made rather than as the way songs go.
Map the structure of your own AT1 song and mark what changes at each boundary.

criteria: I can map a song's structure.
I can say what changes at each section boundary.

lessons.title: The process log opens
lessons.contentPoint: Techniques and structures to refine material
lessons.intention: We are learning to document what we try, not only what we keep.
criteria: I can write a log entry that records a decision and the reason for it.
steps: The process log opens and runs to the end of Year 9. A few sentences per draft: what was tried, what changed, what was kept.
A model log entry written together, then a weak one improved.
Students experiment with two openings for their song and log both.
resources: Process log template in flat.io or the class book.
lessons.enduring: The record of how a work was made is evidence in its own right.

body.lead: We are learning to document what we try, not only what we keep.

clauses.text: The process log opens today and runs to the end of Year 9. A few sentences a draft: what you tried, what changed, what you kept.
One model entry is written together, then a weak one is improved, so you can see the difference between a record and a diary.
Try two different openings for your song and log both of them, including the one you are not going to use.

criteria: I can write a log entry that records a decision.
I can give the reason for the decision.

patched.text: Process log template in flat.io or the class book

lessons.title: Choosing a progression and a groove
lessons.contentPoint: Techniques and structures to refine material
lessons.intention: We are learning to experiment with compositional material before committing to it.
criteria: I can test more than one option and say why I kept the one I kept.
steps: Students choose a progression from a supplied set and a groove to sit it on, then test the pairing.
Experimenting deliberately: the same progression at three tempos and in two metres.
The chosen pairing entered into flat.io from the template.
lessons.enduring: Choosing well means having tried the alternatives.

body.lead: We are learning to experiment with compositional material before committing to it.

clauses.text: A set of progressions and a bank of grooves. You choose one of each and then test whether they actually go together.
Run the same progression at three tempos and in two metres. This is a deliberate experiment, not clicking about.
Enter the pairing you chose into the song template, and log why you kept that one and not the others.

criteria: I can test more than one option.
I can say why I kept the one I kept.

lessons.title: Writing the chorus first
lessons.intention: We are learning to develop musical material inside a fixed structure.
criteria: I can write a chorus melody that fits the progression and lands as a hook.
steps: The chorus written first, because it carries the hook and sets the register for everything else.
Melody written over the chosen progression in flat.io, with the structure template and lyric scaffold supplied.
Peer listening: does the chorus sound like a chorus?
lessons.enduring: Material is developed within a structure, not poured into one afterwards.

body.lead: We are learning to develop musical material inside a fixed structure.

clauses.text: The chorus is written first, because it carries the hook and it sets the register everything else has to live under.
Write the melody over the progression you chose, using the structure template and the lyric scaffold.
Play it to one other person and ask one question only: does that sound like a chorus?

criteria: I can write a chorus melody that fits the progression.
I can make it land as a hook.

lessons.title: What the song is about
lessons.intention: We are learning to communicate a personal or social view through a song.
criteria: I can say what my song is about and show one musical choice that supports it.
steps: The lyric carries a view. Students state in one sentence what their song is about before they write another bar.
Songs from the term's listening examined for the view they carry and how the music supports it.
Lyric drafted against the scaffold and logged.
lessons.enduring: A song says something, and the music has to agree with the words.

body.lead: We are learning to communicate a personal or social view through a song.

clauses.text: Songs from this term's listening examined for the view they carry, and for how the music agrees with the words rather than only sitting underneath them.
Say in one sentence what your song is about before you write another bar, then keep that sentence where you can see it.
Draft the lyric against the scaffold and log what the song is about, in your own words.

criteria: I can say what my song is about.
I can show one musical choice that supports it.

lessons.title: Notating melody over the progression
lessons.contentPoint: Techniques and structures to refine material
lessons.intention: We are learning to notate a melody accurately enough for someone else to play it.
criteria: I can enter a melody in flat.io with correct rhythm and no missing beats.
steps: Note entry in flat.io taken seriously for the first time: rhythm values, rests, ties and where the melody sits against the chord.
Common notation errors identified and fixed in a supplied faulty file.
Students notate the chorus melody accurately and play it back.
lessons.enduring: Notation is a message to a player, so it has to be right.

body.lead: We are learning to notate a melody accurately enough for someone else to play it.

clauses.text: Note entry is taken seriously for the first time: rhythm values, rests, ties, and where the melody sits against the chord underneath it.
A supplied file full of the usual errors is fixed on the board, and every error is named before it is corrected.
Notate your chorus melody, then play it back and check that what you hear is what you meant to write.

criteria: I can enter a melody with correct rhythm.
I can find my own missing beats when I check it back.

lessons.title: The verse, and making it different
lessons.intention: We are learning to develop contrasting material inside one song.
criteria: I can write a verse that is audibly different from my chorus and explain how.
steps: The verse written against the chorus: lower register, less movement, more words. The contrast is the point.
Students compare their verse and chorus and adjust until the difference is audible.
Full structure assembled in flat.io.
lessons.enduring: Contrast between sections is what makes a structure audible.

body.lead: We are learning to develop contrasting material inside one song.

clauses.text: The verse is written against the chorus: lower, less movement, more words. The contrast is the entire point of it.
Assemble the full structure, verse and chorus in order, and listen to it end to end.
Compare your verse with your chorus and keep adjusting until the difference is audible to somebody who has not heard it before.

criteria: I can write a verse that is audibly different from my chorus.
I can explain how it is different.

lessons.title: Lyric and music together
lessons.intention: We are learning to make the music and the words serve the same idea.
criteria: I can adjust my melody so the important words fall in the right place.
steps: Lyric and melody sung together for the first time, and adjusted where the stress falls wrongly.
Does the music support the view the lyric carries? Where it does not, one of the two changes.
Log entry on what changed when the words met the tune.
lessons.enduring: Word stress and musical stress have to agree or the line sounds wrong.

body.lead: We are learning to make the music and the words serve the same idea.

clauses.text: Lyric and melody are sung together for the first time. Where the stress lands on the wrong syllable, you hear it immediately.
Decide whether the music supports the view the lyric carries. Where it does not, one of the two has to change, and you choose which one.
Log what changed when the words met the tune.

criteria: I can adjust my melody so the important words fall in the right place.
I can say which of the two I changed, and why.

lessons.title: Share and log: closing the term
lessons.contentPoint: Techniques and structures to refine material
lessons.intention: We are learning to share unfinished work and use feedback on it.
criteria: I can present a draft, take feedback and record what I would change.
steps: Drafts played to the class, unmarked. Two dot points of feedback each.
Final log entry for the term: what was tried, what was kept, what the student would do differently.
Term closed by naming what Term 2 needs from this work: notation, structure and the log habit.
lessons.enduring: An unassessed share is where risk is cheap, which is why it is here.

body.lead: We are learning to share unfinished work and use the feedback we get on it.

clauses.text: Drafts are played to the class and nothing is marked. Two dot points of feedback each, in the language we have been using all term.
What Term 2 needs from this work is named out loud: notation, structure, and the habit of logging.
Write the last log entry of the term: what you tried, what you kept, and what you would do differently.

criteria: I can present a draft and take feedback on it.
I can record what I would change.
